routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the more adequate account of cosmic intelligibility, rational knowledge, objective morality, human dignity, and enduring hope, while connecting those explanatory claims to the character and revelation of the Christian God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its general theistic explanations remain coherent under naturalistic objections, its specifically Christian claims have an adequate epistemic bridge, and its account of divine greatness addresses evil, coercion, and religious wrongdoing.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian God is worthy of the motion's greatness claim and that Christian theism jointly explains the motion's scientific, moral, dignitary, and hopeful dimensions better than anti-theism.

centralBridges.description: Account for cosmic order, biological information, and trustworthy rational inquiry through an intelligent creator without treating scientific mechanisms as competing creator explanations.
Ground objective moral obligation and distinctive human worth in God rather than in wholly blind natural processes.
Supply a warranted transition from general creator claims to Christianity through claims about Jesus, revelation, resurrection, and atonement.
Reconcile divine greatness with suffering, judgment, freedom, and allegations that supernatural authority is intrinsically tyrannical.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish conduct that follows Christian teaching from violence or oppression committed by professed adherents contrary to that teaching.
Relate Christian commitments to liberty, conscience, rights, education, and reform without making historical association substitute for the central truth claims.

routes.description: Defeat the claimed explanatory and moral advantages of Christian theism by advancing naturalistic and secular alternatives, challenging the evidential bridge to revelation, and arguing that the proposed divine rule is neither necessary nor worthy of worship.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if natural and human explanations cover the motion's principal domains without God, specifically Christian claims remain insufficiently warranted, and suffering, authority, atonement, or religion's effects defeat the attribution of divine greatness.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christian theism neither provides the better explanation across the motion's domains nor establishes a God whose character and governance satisfy the claim of greatness.

centralBridges.description: Defend evidence-responsive natural inquiry and show that adding divine agency does not improve explanations of cosmic or biological phenomena.
Explain morality, solidarity, dignity, meaning, and hope through human social, evolutionary, intellectual, and cultural resources without supernatural premises.
Require adequate evidence for knowledge of divine intentions and contest the historical, prophetic, and miraculous basis of specifically Christian revelation.
Show how suffering, surveillance, punishment, coercion, or vicarious redemption conflicts with the asserted goodness and greatness of the Christian God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish whether religious violence and oppression arise from supernatural doctrines themselves rather than merely from their misuse.
Test claims of Christian moral or political progress against religious complicity, nonreligious reform, and competing explanations of totalitarianism.

sections.title: Cosmic Intelligibility, Biology, and Natural Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the motion's science dimension by comparing creator-based explanations of order, intelligibility, and biological information with naturalistic standards of evidence and explanatory sufficiency.

sections.title: Reason, Revelation, and the Warrant for Christianity
sections.rationale: The motion concerns Christian theism rather than an unspecified first cause, making the epistemic transition from cosmic order to divine intentions, Jesus's identity, miracles, prophecy, and resurrection indispensable.

sections.title: Morality, Objective Obligation, and Atonement
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether God is required to ground moral truth and responsibility, whether secular accounts can sustain moral judgment, and whether distinctively Christian sacrifice coheres morally.

sections.title: Human Dignity, Meaning, Solidarity, and Hope
sections.rationale: The issue directly covers three named burdens by testing divine-image and ultimate-hope accounts against evolutionary, social, cultural, and secular accounts of human worth and purpose.

sections.title: Divine Greatness, Suffering, Freedom, and Authority
sections.rationale: Because the motion expressly asks whether God is great, the implications of natural evil, judgment, omniscience, freedom, redemption, and divine governance form a distinct motion-level clash.

sections.title: Religion, Violence, Liberty, and Historical Consequences
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether coercion and social harm follow from Christian or supernatural commitments and how claims about rights, reform, slavery, fascism, and totalitarianism bear on religion's consequences.
